Andean Region.regional_narrative:
The Andean region in Q3 2026 is a study in bifurcation: two macro-stable, investment-grade-adjacent economies (Peru, Ecuador) running current-account surpluses and single-digit inflation sit alongside two economies in acute distress (Bolivia, Venezuela) where debt-to-GDP ratios have spiraled past 100% and inflation is measured in double or triple digits, with Colombia occupying an uneasy middle ground of fiscal slippage atop still-functioning capital markets. Peru's current account surplus (3.6% of GDP, World Bank 2025) and rock-bottom government debt (30% of GDP, IMF 2026) make it the region's fiscal anchor, while Ecuador posts the region's strongest external position (5.9% current account surplus) and near-full employment (3.3% unemployment) even as its homicide rate climbs to Latin America's highest. Bolivia and Venezuela, by contrast, illustrate what happens when subsidy regimes and currency pegs break under pressure: Bolivia's boliviano de-pegged on June 26, 2026 amid GDP contracting 3.3% and debt jumping from 84.8% to 102.7% of GDP (IMF), while Venezuela's inflation print of 387.4% (IMF, 2026) coexists with a debt stock at 308.7% of GDP -- yet its oil sector is simultaneously reopening to Chevron and Shell capital.

What ties the region together is that political transition risk is now sitting directly on top of otherwise-legible macro stories in three of five countries simultaneously: Peru's contested July 2026 presidential proclamation, Colombia's razor-thin transition to Abelardo de la Espriella, and Venezuela's earthquake-battered interim government all mean capital allocators must price sovereign and institutional risk that is orthogonal to, not derived from, the underlying growth and external-balance data. Meanwhile, the region's extractives pipeline -- Peru's $6.3 billion projected 2026 mining capex, Ecuador's $11 billion cadastre reopening, Bolivia's lithium-code rewrite, and Venezuela's Orinoco Belt IOC re-entry -- suggests global capital is willing to look through near-term political noise toward copper, gold, and heavy-crude fundamentals that remain structurally attractive.

Capital-flow dynamics reinforce the divergence: Colombia's FDI has fallen to a five-year low even as its multilateral infrastructure pipeline (World Bank PPI records over $3.8 billion in active transport/toll-road concessions) continues largely undisturbed, while Peru's mining-linked investment accelerated 43.5% year-on-year in early 2026. The region, in short, offers investors a menu where fiscal orthodoxy (Peru, Ecuador) and fiscal emergency (Bolivia, Venezuela) trade at opposite ends of the same commodity cycle, with Colombia's PPP infrastructure market the one segment insulated from the political cycle roiling its presidency.

Andean Region.risk_outlook: The single largest risk to the Andean outlook is that political and institutional stress is concentrated in the same window across three of five countries: Peru's Fujimori-Sánchez proclamation dispute now sits before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights with a newly reconstituted Senate yet to prove it can break the pattern of nine presidents in ten years; Colombia's transition to de la Espriella is razor-thin and historically contested against a backdrop of fiscal slippage; and Venezuela's interim government under Delcy Rodríguez is managing a death toll past 3,000 from the June earthquakes while trying to sustain an oil reopening. Bolivia adds a distinct but compounding risk in the form of unresolved social conflict -- at least 17 dead in May-June protests -- layered on a currency de-peg and debt trajectory that could still deteriorate further before mining-code reforms become bankable. Ecuador's security backdrop, with the highest homicide rate in Latin America and a bombing of its own mining regulator, is the clearest case where a constructive macro and financing story could be undermined by on-the-ground execution risk rather than balance-sheet fundamentals. Collectively, these are not diversified idiosyncratic risks but a correlated regional pattern of institutional fragility arriving at the same moment as several genuine capital-formation catalysts, and principals should size positions with that correlation, not just individual country risk, in mind.

Central Africa.regional_narrative:
Central Africa in mid-2026 is a region of two economies operating on entirely different clocks. The CEMAC hydrocarbon states — Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, and Republic of Congo — are managing legacy debt loads (86.1%, 39.1%, and 91.3% of GDP respectively, IMF 2026) against flat-to-negative growth, while the region's two frontier giants, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic, are posting the fastest growth in the bloc (5.9% and 2.6% IMF-projected 2026 real GDP growth) precisely where security risk is most acute. Cameroon sits between these poles: a modestly stabilizing macro picture (3.3% growth, inflation easing to 3.4-3.5%, debt at a comparatively manageable 39.3% of GDP) overlaid on an elite succession crisis and dispersed insurgent activity that current event-count data likely understates.

The capital-flows story reinforces this split. FDI intensity is inversely correlated with fiscal comfort: Gabon draws the region's strongest FDI-to-GDP ratio (5.5%, World Bank 2024) even as it deprograms nearly CFAF 968 billion in public investment for lacking feasibility studies, while DRC and Republic of Congo both pull in 3.8% of GDP in FDI against improving (DRC) or precarious (Congo) fiscal backdrops. Equatorial Guinea is the outlier on every axis — a third consecutive year of GDP contraction (-2.7% projected 2026) coinciding with visible elite fracture inside the ruling family, yet still drawing fresh upstream exploration commitments (EG Ronda 2026, Eni). The throughline for the region as a whole is that hydrocarbons and mining remain the primary vector connecting Central Africa to global capital, with infrastructure concessions (ports, power, telecom towers) serving as the secondary, steadily recurring channel of private participation regardless of which country's politics are in flux.

For a portfolio principal, the region rewards a barbell approach: exposure to the hydrocarbon/mining engines that generate hard-currency earnings almost irrespective of domestic political noise (Congo's offshore oil, DRC's copper belt, Equatorial Guinea's licensing rounds), paired with selective infrastructure plays where multilateral or DFC-grade financing has already de-risked the entry point (Gabon's PPI pipeline, DRC's mini-grid and port concessions). The unifying regional risk is that none of the six states offers a genuinely clean macro-security combination — CAR and DRC pair strong growth with active conflict; Gabon and Congo pair political calm with balance-sheet fragility; Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea pair moderate-to-poor macro readings with rising elite instability.

FDI net inflows of 3.8% of GDP (World Bank, 2024) confirm that international capital continues to price DRC's mineral endowment ahead of its security headline risk, concentrated overwhelmingly in copper and cobalt extraction in the south, geographically distinct from the conflict-affected east.

Central Africa.risk_outlook: The region's principal risk is that macro improvement and security/governance deterioration are running in parallel rather than in sequence, meaning good headline numbers cannot be read as a proxy for operational safety anywhere in Central Africa. DRC's strengthening growth and fiscal metrics sit against an escalating Rwanda dispute now at the ICJ and an Ebola outbreak that had surpassed 500 deaths by early July 2026; CAR's genuine national-level political normalization (a completed transition, government seated by May 2026) coexists with worsening armed-group violence and targeted killings in Vakaga, Haut-Mbomou, and Mbomou; and Cameroon's stabilizing inflation and debt figures mask an unresolved presidential succession question and geographically dispersed Anglophone and Boko Haram/ISWAP activity that structured conflict tallies likely understate. Layered on top is a fiscal-fragility risk specific to the CEMAC oil states: Gabon and Republic of Congo are both carrying government debt above 85% of GDP with Congo's budget surplus having collapsed to 0.9% of GDP, leaving little room for policy error should oil prices or investor sentiment turn, while Equatorial Guinea's simultaneous economic contraction and intra-ruling-family friction over resource control represents the sharpest single-country deterioration in the region.

Central America & Caribbean.regional_narrative:
Central America and the Caribbean in Q3 2026 is a region of two distinct growth speeds separated by a widening security-and-solvency chasm, with capital increasingly rewarding the "northern triangle plus" cluster of Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua alongside the Dominican Republic and Costa Rica, while Haiti, Cuba and Jamaica illustrate three very different ways a small open economy can be knocked off course. IMF 2026 projections show Guatemala (3.9%), Nicaragua (3.8%), Panama (3.8%) and the Dominican Republic (3.7%) all growing faster than the US or the euro area, with inflation largely tamed -- Guatemala at 2.6%, Nicaragua at 3.5%, Costa Rica actually in mild deflation at -0.4% -- and government debt loads in Guatemala (27.6% of GDP) and Nicaragua (33.2%) that remain the envy of far larger emerging markets (IMF, 2026). This is a region where fiscal orthodoxy and IMF program engagement (Honduras's May 2026 EFF/ECF staff-level agreement unlocking roughly $245 million) coexist with negative real interest-rate discipline that has kept inflation low even as global commodity and freight costs stayed elevated.

The more important story for a portfolio principal, however, is that macro stability and institutional/political stability have decoupled almost everywhere in the region simultaneously. Nicaragua pairs a 4.9% 2025 growth rate and a current account surplus with declining FDI/GDP since 2022 and a regime that has gone unrefreshed by Western development finance since FY2018. Panama pairs 3.8% IMF growth with a 63.1% collapse in FDI in 2025 tied to the unresolved Cobre Panamá concession and Canal-adjacent US-China port friction. Costa Rica pairs a tourism boom (eight consecutive months of arrivals growth, 9.4% y/y air-tourist growth through May 2026) with a live executive-judiciary confrontation over alleged organized-crime infiltration of the courts. Honduras pairs IMF program credibility with a contested presidential election and an unresolved $1.6 billion Próspera ISDS claim. Even the Dominican Republic's genuinely clean growth story -- 4.1% y/y Q1 2026 growth, a fourth consecutive record FDI year at $5.03 billion, 6.6 million tourist arrivals in H1 2026 -- is partly obscured by GDELT data noise that overstates its conflict signal.

At the other end of the spectrum, Haiti and Cuba represent genuine tail risk rather than noise: Haiti's economy is IMF-projected to contract 1.7% in 2026 (a seventh consecutive contraction) with inflation above 23%, roughly 2,300 gang-related deaths and 1.5 million displaced in 2026 alone, and a transitional government upheaval weeks before August 30 elections; Cuba faces a 7.2% projected 2026 GDP contraction, recurring nationwide blackouts, and a June 2026 Visa/Mastercard cutoff that signals deepening financial isolation. Jamaica sits in between -- a -1.2% 2026 growth projection and a swing to a roughly -6.0%-of-GDP current account deficit driven by Hurricane Melissa and oil-price pressure, but explicitly characterized by officials as a weather-and-terms-of-trade shock rather than a structural or governance crisis.

Central America & Caribbean.risk_outlook: The region's dominant risk is that political and institutional fragility is now surfacing almost everywhere growth looks strongest, not just in the obvious distress cases. Honduras's contested November 2025 election, a president polling at 31% approval after 100 days, and the unresolved $1.6 billion Próspera ISDS claim sit atop an otherwise IMF-endorsed macro program; Costa Rica's executive-judiciary confrontation over alleged organized-crime infiltration of the courts is unaccompanied by unrest but signals real institutional stress; Panama's Cobre Panamá concession and Canal-adjacent US-China port friction help explain a 63.1% FDI collapse that headline growth figures obscure; and Nicaragua's macro stability sits alongside international sanctions, declining FDI since 2022, and no Western development-finance refresh since FY2018. At the acute end, Haiti's security collapse (roughly 2,300 gang-related deaths and 1.5 million displaced in 2026) and a prime-ministerial ouster weeks before August 30 elections, alongside Cuba's compounding energy-grid failures and financial-network isolation (the June 2026 Visa/Mastercard cutoff), represent binding constraints that could deteriorate further with little warning. Jamaica's hurricane-and-oil-price shock is the one clear case genuinely bounded by external, non-structural factors, but a repeat storm season or renewed oil-price spike from Middle East tensions would test that characterization. Across the board, principals should treat headline conflict-event tagging with caution -- both Panama's and the Dominican Republic's data show substantial misattribution from unrelated foreign news stories -- while still taking the country-specific, verified political and legal signals (Próspera, Cobre Panamá, Costa Rica's court dispute, Nicaragua's sanctions status) seriously as the primary sources of tail risk.

East Africa / Horn.regional_narrative:
East Africa and the Horn in mid-2026 present the sharpest growth-versus-governance divergence of any African sub-region: five economies -- Ethiopia (9.2%), Rwanda (7.2%), Uganda (7.5%), Djibouti (6.0%) and Tanzania (5.9%) -- are posting IMF-projected 2026 real GDP growth rates that would rank among the fastest globally, while political and security conditions in the same countries (and their immediate neighbors) are deteriorating in ways the growth data does not capture. Ethiopia's fifth ECF review completion and falling debt (40.4% of GDP) sit alongside an insurgency CSIS expects to intensify post-election; Uganda's 10.2%-growth budget, financed in part by first oil revenue as EACOP nears completion, sits alongside the abduction of an opposition lawyer and a UN Secretary-General statement on unresolved detentions; Tanzania's contained inflation (3.3-4.0%) and falling debt (48.7% of GDP) sit beside a reimposed rally ban and pre-protest arrests. The region's macro strength is real, but it is increasingly a strength that coexists with, rather than displaces, political risk.

A second, starker divergence separates this "growth cohort" from a fragile cohort -- Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and Eritrea -- where conflict is not a backdrop to the macro story but the macro story itself. Sudan's war has pushed inflation near 75%, debt above 169% of GDP, and shifted its center of gravity to Kordofan, where UN-documented strikes have killed dozens and displaced thousands; formal capital flows there are effectively frozen, historical Chinese grants aside. South Sudan's peace process is formally advancing (a December 22, 2026 election date is now locked in) even as UNMISS recorded 767 civilian deaths in three months and SPLM-IO has threatened to treat voter registration as an act of war. Somalia's federal offensive against al-Shabaab continues alongside fraying federal-state cohesion and a weakening of the AU peacekeeping-financing architecture. This bifurcation means regional aggregates are almost meaningless: capital allocators need country-specific, not regional, risk budgets.

Capital flows corroborate the split. FDI as a share of GDP is strongest precisely where security risk is elevated or where the base is tiny -- Uganda (6.0%), Somalia (6.4%), Rwanda (3.8%) -- while Kenya, the region's deepest capital market, draws just 0.4% of GDP in FDI even as its debt climbs to 71.6% of GDP and its current account deficit widens to -4.1%. Kenya's own instability-to-investment correlation (unrest predicting a rise in investment activity three months later, r=0.575 across 63 months) suggests investors have learned to read Kenyan unrest as a stabilization-financing signal rather than a pure risk-off trigger -- a dynamic worth testing against the Saba Saba-period tension now building. Meanwhile Burundi's IMF-documented disinflation (45% to 8.6% in twelve months) shows that even the region's most fragile economies can stabilize quickly under credible policy, though reserve cover of just 1.6 months of imports shows how thin that stabilization remains.

Mexico.regional_narrative:
Mexico's macro story in Q3 2026 is one of stabilizing aggregates masking an increasingly bifurcated real economy. Headline growth has decelerated sharply from the boom years of the nearshoring narrative -- World Bank data show GDP growth of just 0.6% in 2025, with the IMF projecting a modest recovery to 1.6% in 2026 -- even as inflation has eased to 3.8-3.9% (World Bank, IMF) and unemployment sits near historic lows at 2.6-2.7%. This is not a crisis economy: the current account deficit is a manageable 0.4% of GDP (2025) and FDI inflows still run at 2.5% of GDP (2024, World Bank), evidence that capital continues to find a home in the country even as the growth engine sputters.

The more important story for a portfolio principal is beneath the aggregates. Mexico's investment case is fracturing by sector rather than moving as a single bloc. Traditional automotive manufacturing -- the poster child of the post-2020 nearshoring thesis -- is showing concrete signs of reversal, most visibly in Toyota's $3.6 billion Texas plant investment that relocates Tacoma pickup production away from Mexican soil (CBS News, July 7, 2026). At the same time, renewable energy, ICT/data-center infrastructure, and fintech/SME lending continue to attract diversified private and DFC capital, largely undisturbed by the manufacturing malaise. Government debt has also crept up to 62.7% of GDP (IMF, 2026), a level that bears watching as fiscal space narrows against a backdrop of slower growth and rising security spending.

Taken together, Mexico in 2026 looks less like a single nearshoring story and more like two economies moving in different directions: a manufacturing-and-trade-integration complex under real stress from both U.S. reshoring competition and intensifying domestic security risk, and a digital/energy-infrastructure complex that remains genuinely investable on its own merits. Distinguishing between the two is the central task of any Mexico allocation thesis right now.

North Africa.regional_narrative:
North Africa in mid-2026 is a region of two speeds and one shared vulnerability. Morocco and Egypt are executing genuine macro-stabilization and diversification programs — Morocco with IMF-projected 4.9% real GDP growth, inflation pinned near 1%, and a public debt ratio easing from 67.1% to 65.8% of GDP, while automotive exports overtake phosphates as the kingdom's top goods export (Stimson Center, HCP); Egypt with inflation cooling from over 20% to a projected 13.2% (IMF), reserves past $53bn (Middle East Observer, May 2026), and a 20.7% year-to-date EGX30 rally rewarding the seventh EFF review's staff-level agreement. Algeria and Tunisia sit a notch behind on the reform curve — Algeria growing near 3.8% with inflation easing sharply and its first sovereign Sukuk welcomed by the IMF, but paired with a rising public-debt trajectory and a July parliamentary election that drew only ~21% turnout after mass candidate disqualification; Tunisia stuck in a stalled IMF program, financing its 84.9%-of-GDP debt load through a planned ~€2 billion 2026 market raise and zero-interest central-bank deficit financing that analysts flag as inflationary. Libya, meanwhile, is the region's outlier on both axes: 13.4% headline 2025 growth and a 6.7% IMF 2026 projection reflect an oil-recovery low base, and a June tripartite roadmap toward February 2027 elections plus the first unified state budget since 2013 (~$30bn) mark the most credible political opening in years — even as security-sector unification lags visibly behind the political and fiscal tracks.

The region's capital-flow story is genuinely bifurcated. Egypt is pulling in FDI equivalent to 12.0% of GDP (World Bank, 2024) — a scale utterly unmatched by its neighbors (Morocco 1.1%, Tunisia 1.5%, Libya 1.8%, Algeria 0.5%) — concentrated in Gulf-backed privatization, renewables, and Suez-corridor logistics. Morocco compensates with a diversifying industrial base (autos, and now over $700M in Chinese battery-materials commitments) rather than raw FDI volume. Algeria and Libya remain hydrocarbon- and connectivity-infrastructure plays with comparatively thin non-energy inflows. A common thread across all five is a renewable-energy and connectivity project pipeline — solar, wind, desalination, and the shared MEDUSA submarine cable — that gives the region a bankable greenfield template independent of each country's political trajectory.

The single dynamic an executive must hold in mind: North Africa's growth and reform momentum in 2026 is running in parallel with, not immune from, regional and domestic political risk — Egypt's stabilization sits beside an intensifying Israel-Iran-Hezbollah conflict theater on its doorstep, Libya's fiscal-political opening sits beside unresolved militia fault lines, Algeria's macro improvement sits beside an eroding electoral-legitimacy signal, and Tunisia's fragile fiscal equilibrium sits beside a tightening political space around President Saied. None of these is a base-case derailment, but each is a live tail risk layered onto an otherwise constructive regional growth story.

Southern Africa.regional_narrative:
Southern Africa in Q3 2026 is a region of striking macro-political divergence layered atop a shared structural theme: an energy and critical-minerals investment supercycle is financing itself even as fiscal space narrows almost everywhere else. At one pole sits South Africa, where three consecutive rating agencies upgraded or improved the sovereign outlook between May and June 2026 on the back of a third straight primary fiscal surplus (Moody's, S&P, Fitch), yet growth remains stuck near 1.0-1.1% (IMF/World Bank) and unemployment above 32% — a combination that detonated into nationwide anti-migrant unrest requiring a 3,000-plus troop deployment in June-July 2026. At the other pole, Zimbabwe has engineered a genuine disinflation, with IMF data showing price growth collapsing from 81.4% in 2025 to a projected 8.0% in 2026 alongside 5.0% real GDP growth, even as a constitutional tenure-extension bill has fractured the ruling elite. The region's growth dispersion is unusually wide for a single bloc: Zimbabwe at 5.0% and Botswana at 4.7% (IMF 2026 projections) sit against outright contractions in Mozambique (-0.5% World Bank 2025) and Botswana's own -0.7% 2025 print, with South Africa, Namibia, and Lesotho all clustered in the 1-2.4% range that barely outpaces population growth.

The second regional story is capital-flow bifurcation around hydrocarbons and critical minerals. Mozambique and Namibia post the two largest FDI-to-GDP ratios in the bloc — 15.4% and 14.2% respectively (World Bank, 2024) — almost entirely explained by LNG and offshore oil buildouts (TotalEnergies' $20bn Mozambique LNG restart, an expected ExxonMobil Rovuma FID by September 2026, and bp's move to operate three Walvis Basin blocks in Namibia per the African Energy Chamber). Yet both economies are simultaneously running the region's widest current-account deficits — Mozambique's projected at -43.0% of GDP for 2026 and Namibia's widening to -15.7% — and carry debt loads of 106.1% and 70.5% of GDP (IMF), underscoring that the capex boom is financed as much by external drawdown as by domestic strength. Zambia offers the clearest counter-narrative of stabilization-by-restructuring: inflation down to 6.5% by June 2026 (lowest since February 2018), reserves rebuilt to 4.4 months of import cover, and roughly 94% of its debt-restructuring perimeter now resolved, though its primary surplus is set to narrow sharply from 3.1% to 1.1% of GDP in 2026, right into an approaching election.

The third thread is renewable-energy financing as the one asset class every country in the bloc — regardless of fiscal or political condition — continues to attract. From Angola's $1.6bn Sun Africa solar-and-mini-grid portfolio to Zambia's Itimpi and Serenje solar plants, Malawi's blended-finance Golomoti plant, Lesotho's multi-financier Ramarothole-to-ASCENT pipeline, Eswatini's Frazium and Lower Maguduza projects, and South Africa's Oya/Oasis/Mogobe/Virginia pipeline, utility-scale power is the connective tissue of Southern African project finance in 2026, a pattern the region's own investment thesis links directly to South Africa's sovereign-upgrade cycle lowering regional infrastructure financing costs.

Southern Cone.regional_narrative:
The Southern Cone in Q3 2026 tells a story of macro convergence masking political divergence. Argentina and Brazil, the region's two largest economies, are both mid-stabilization: Argentine inflation has collapsed from 211% at end-2023 to an IMF-projected 30.4% in 2026, while government debt eases to 70.4% of GDP, and Brazil's IMF Article IV mission (June 1, 2026) calls that economy "remarkably resilient" even as growth cools to 1.9% and debt climbs to 96.5% of GDP. Chile is mid-cycle, with growth slowing to an IMF-projected 1.8% in 2026 before a copper-price-driven rebound to 2.6% in 2027, while Paraguay stands out as the region's clear growth outlier, posting 6.6% GDP growth in 2025 — its strongest in twelve years, per President Peña — alongside contained government debt near 38% of GDP and inflation moderating to 3.3%. Uruguay, by contrast, is the region's stability anchor turned political question mark: solid 1.8% growth and 66.8% debt-to-GDP sit uneasily against a president whose approval has collapsed to 20%.

The cross-country pattern that matters most for capital allocation is the decoupling of macro fundamentals from political capital across nearly every country in the bloc. Argentina's disinflation is real but running alongside President Milei's approval slide to 36% and a Cabinet reshuffle; Chile's copper-linked recovery case is intact but priced against a new president already at roughly 40% approval within a hundred days; Uruguay's institutional stability brand is being tested by a widening ethics scandal. Brazil is the partial exception — its governance stress (the Banco Master fraud probe, organized-crime enforcement in its two largest metros) is genuine but distinct from headline political-violence noise, much of which automated feeds mischaracterize. Paraguay alone combines strong macro with a quiet security backdrop, its governance risks narrow and name-specific (targeted U.S. Treasury sanctions) rather than systemic.

Capital flows reflect this bifurcation: Chile's peso bond market drew record foreign inflows in 2026 on central bank rate cuts, and Brazil remains a contested financing destination between Chinese state financiers (China Development Bank, ICBC, China Eximbank) and a smaller U.S. DFC footprint, particularly around grid and Petrobras-linked infrastructure. FDI intensity diverges sharply too — Chile at 4.0% of GDP and Brazil at 3.4% lead, while Uruguay's negative net FDI reading (-4.8% of GDP, 2024) is a genuine outlier worth flagging even as its underlying project pipeline (toll roads, transmission, tourism real estate) continues to attract capital.

West Africa / Sahel.regional_narrative:
West Africa and the Sahel in mid-2026 are two economies wearing one map. The coastal and resource belt -- Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire, Benin, Ghana, Senegal, Niger -- is delivering some of the strongest real growth numbers in the developing world, with IMF 2026 projections of 8.7% in Guinea, 7.0% in Benin, 6.7% in Niger, and 6.2% in Côte d'Ivoire, underwritten by iron-ore, gold, oil, uranium and a genuinely deep pipeline of World Bank PPI-tracked power and port financing. Layered on top, however, is a security and governance map that no longer tracks national borders: JNIM and ISSP-linked violence has moved from the deep Sahel interior (Mali's fall of Kidal to the FLA/JNIM in April 2026, coordinated Niger attacks on Inates, Banibangou and Niamey airport in June) into direct cross-border strikes on Beninese and Ivorian military positions and Nigerian installations, while Chad absorbs Sudan-war spillover at Tiné. The core regional insight is that macro indicators -- inflation, debt, growth -- are increasingly lagging indicators of political risk here; open-web and specialist reporting, not structured data, is currently the more reliable barometer in Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Nigeria.

Capital flows corroborate a bifurcation rather than a uniform frontier story. FDI is concentrated and large in resource-and-energy plays -- Mauritania (13.2% of GDP, Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas), Liberia (9.9%) and Gambia (9.7%) all post FDI ratios that dwarf Nigeria's anemic 0.6%, underscoring that scale of economy is no longer the region's main draw; project bankability is. Guinea's Simandou-linked buildout, Côte d'Ivoire's $209 billion National Development Plan (70% private-capital participation, announced July 2026), and a genuinely repeatable West African solar-greenfield financing template spanning Benin, Togo, Chad, Burkina Faso and Senegal all point to power-sector infrastructure as the region's most consistently bankable theme regardless of political regime type -- financing has continued even through Burkina Faso's and Mali's juntas and diplomatic ruptures.

The other defining regional dynamic is fiscal divergence among the states considered "stable." Nigeria's inflation re-accelerated to near 16% in 2026 IMF terms (15.93% in the open-web May print) on an oil-shock pass-through even as its debt-to-GDP eases to 32.3%; Ghana is disinflating sharply (14.2% to a projected 5.8%) while its debt still climbs toward 53% of GDP; and Senegal's 132.3% debt-to-GDP alongside a still-deteriorating current account marks it as the region's clearest fiscal outlier, its risk now concentrated in a live constitutional referendum rather than street violence. For portfolio principals, the region rewards granular country and sector selection over broad frontier-Africa beta -- the same "West Africa" label now spans an 8.7%-growth mining boom and a five-town jihadist offensive within a single quarter.

West Africa / Sahel.risk_outlook: The region's central risk is that jihadist violence linked to JNIM, ISSP and affiliated networks has stopped respecting the boundary between "Sahel interior" and "coastal stable" states: Mali's loss of Kidal and assassination of its Defence Minister, Niger's airport-targeting attacks in Niamey (the third such incident in the Sahel in six months per ACLED), and cross-border strikes now reaching Beninese and Ivorian military positions together suggest a contagion dynamic rather than contained national insurgencies. Compounding this, three of the region's most militarily exposed states -- Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger -- are also those where juntas have moved to close civic space (118 Burkinabè NGOs dissolved) and sever traditional Western security partnerships (Burkina Faso-France rupture, Chad's reported reversal on French force expulsion), leaving China as an increasingly dominant, but comparatively opaque, external financing partner across the Sahel bloc. Layered on top are country-specific fiscal and political fault lines that could independently derail sentiment: Senegal's 132.3% debt-to-GDP and live constitutional referendum, Nigeria's inflation re-acceleration on external oil-shock pass-through, and governance-credibility tests in Liberia (the Roberts airport cocaine seizure implicating national security leadership) and Gambia (a resigned Chief of Defence Staff amid corruption allegations ahead of a December 2026 election). None of these individually threatens the region's growth headline, but their simultaneity argues that principals should treat West Africa's strong aggregate GDP numbers as a poor proxy for the security and governance dispersion beneath them.
